items.prompt: Given a pointer to a node, splicing it out of a doubly linked list is typically?
whyWrong: You do not rescan from the head if you already hold the node (and its neighbors).

items.prompt: Reaching the i-th node from the head of a singly linked list costs?
whyWrong: There is no address arithmetic like an array.
Binary lifting is not the basic list story.
Amortization does not make a single walk constant.

items.prompt: Detect a cycle in a linked list with O(1) extra space. Classic tool?
choices: Convert to array then binary search
items.whyRight: Slow and fast meet iff a cycle exists.
whyWrong: Hashing works but uses linear space.
Arrays and binary search are a different representation.

items.prompt: Why are middle inserts cheaper on a list than on an array once you hold the neighbor?
choices: No need to shift a contiguous tail
Lists always have O(1) index access
Cache lines never matter for arrays
items.whyRight: A list rewires pointers; an array must move every later element.
whyWrong: Index access on a list is still a walk.
Cache usually favors arrays; that does not erase the shift cost.

items.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively. What do you update each step?
choices: next pointers while walking, keeping prev/curr
Only the head reference once at the end
A stack of values then rebuild as an array
items.whyRight: Each node’s next flips to the previous node.
whyWrong: One head update cannot reverse all links.
Value stacks miss the pointer-rewriting lesson.
Random rewiring is not an algorithm.

items.prompt: Interview prompt: “delete a node in O(1) given only that node” on a singly list (not tail). Trick?
choices: Copy the next node’s value into this node, then bypass next
Allocate a new list without that value
It is impossible without the head always
items.whyRight: You cannot easily fix the previous next without prev; copying next fakes the delete.
whyWrong: Walking from head is O(n) and needs the head.
The classic trick exists for non-tail nodes.
